evidence.claim: Forested Ouachita valleys link railroad Heavener with former timber towns
evidence.quote: The byway winds through the forested valleys of the Ouachita Mountains

evidence.claim: railroad Heavener
evidence.quote: In 1896 the Kansas City, Pittsburg and Gulf Railroad built tracks through the town.

evidence.claim: former timber towns
evidence.quote: the Buschow mill, a victim of its own "cut and move on" timber policies, closed in 1932

evidence.claim: Mountain Gateway follows US 59/270 for 22 miles from Heavener to the Arkansas line, winding through forested Ouachita valleys.
evidence.quote: The Mountain Gateway Scenic Byway in southeast Oklahoma follows Hwy 59/270 for 22 miles between Heavener and the Arkansas state line. The byway winds through the forested valleys of the Ouachita Mountains

evidence.claim: The paved, two-lane road has steep grades and sharp curves.
evidence.quote: The Mountain Gateway Scenic Byway is a two-lane paved road with some steep grades and sharp curves.

evidence.claim: Oklahoma’s tourism department presents this scenic byway as a route through the Winding Stair Mountain National Recreation Area, with spring wildflowers and neighboring wilderness for walking and riding.
evidence.quote: The byway winds through the forested valleys of the Ouachita Mountains and the 26,445-acre Winding Stair Mountain National Recreation area.

evidence.claim: with spring wildflowers and neighboring wilderness for walking and riding.
evidence.quote: Wildflowers in the spring proudly display their colors, while autumn also puts on its own beautiful show.

evidence.claim: neighboring wilderness for walking and riding.
evidence.quote: Wilderness areas adjacent to the byway offer seclusion for hikers, backpackers and horseback riders.

evidence.claim: Railroads and mills shaped the places along this drive.
evidence.quote: In 1896 the Kansas City, Pittsburg and Gulf Railroad built tracks through the town.

evidence.claim: Heavener’s railway arrived in 1896; farther south, the settlement later called Stapp began as Thomasville in 1897.
evidence.quote: The community originally formed in 1897 in Indian Territory under the name of Thomasville

evidence.claim: King-Ryder Lumber built a mill and a railway connecting Thomasville with other lines at Howe.
evidence.quote: the King-Ryder Lumber Company, which built a lumber mill at Thomasville and even a railway, the Kingston and Choctaw Valley Railroad, which ran from Thomasville to connect to other rail lines at Howe, Oklahoma.

evidence.claim: A later Buschow mill closed in 1932 after its cut-and-move-on timber operations, and Stapp’s post office followed in 1944.
evidence.quote: the Buschow mill, a victim of its own "cut and move on" timber policies, closed in 1932, and the post office followed in 1944.

evidence.claim: Heavener’s railway arrived in 1896
evidence.quote: In 1896 the Kansas City, Pittsburg and Gulf Railroad built tracks through the town.

evidence.claim: Heavener’s post office and station began in boxcars: one became the post office in May 1896 and another the station.
evidence.quote: A post office was established in a boxcar on May 12, 1896, while another boxcar became the train station.

evidence.claim: That year, the Kansas City, Pittsburg and Gulf Railroad laid tracks through town.
evidence.quote: In 1896 the Kansas City, Pittsburg and Gulf Railroad built tracks through the town.

evidence.claim: Kansas City Southern bought the line in 1900 and added a roundhouse in 1910, making Heavener a division point.
evidence.quote: in 1900 when the Kansas City Southern Railway purchased the rail line. The company established a roundhouse in 1910, making Heavener a division point.

evidence.claim: Rail work continues here: CPKC operates a major yard, a crew base and a fueling facility.
evidence.quote: The CPKC railroad operates a major yard, crew base, and fueling facility in Heavener.

evidence.claim: The town lay in the Choctaw Nation’s Moshulatubbee District through Oklahoma statehood in 1907.
evidence.quote: At the time of its founding, and through Oklahoma's statehood in 1907, Heavener was located in Sugar Loaf County, one of the counties making up the Moshulatubbee District of the Choctaw Nation.

evidence.claim: Nothing remains of old Stapp, a settlement whose fortunes followed successive sawmills.
evidence.quote: nothing remains of the old town today.

evidence.claim: It began as Thomasville in Indian Territory in 1897, about the time Long-Bell Lumber acquired property here.
evidence.quote: The community originally formed in 1897 in Indian Territory under the name of Thomasville, about the time the Long-Bell Lumber Company purchased property there.

evidence.claim: Its subsidiary King-Ryder built both a mill and the Kingston and Choctaw Valley Railroad to connect with lines at Howe.
evidence.quote: the King-Ryder Lumber Company, which built a lumber mill at Thomasville and even a railway, the Kingston and Choctaw Valley Railroad, which ran from Thomasville to connect to other rail lines at Howe, Oklahoma.

evidence.claim: King-Ryder left about 1901, but other timber operators followed.
evidence.quote: King-Ryder left about 1901 for Bon Ami, Louisiana, but other timber operations continued in the area.

evidence.claim: Reborn as Stapp, the settlement gained a Buschow sawmill and a post office.
evidence.quote: The settlement was later reborn as Stapp, and had a Buschow Lumber Company sawmill.  Stapp had a post office beginning in 1918.

evidence.claim: The mill closed in 1932; the post office lasted until 1944.
evidence.quote: closed in 1932, and the post office followed in 1944.

evidence.claim: Page stands on US 59 and 270, 5.5 miles west of the Arkansas border.
evidence.quote: Page is located along U.S. routes 59 and 270, 5.5 miles (8.9 km) west of the Arkansas border.

evidence.claim: Its post office opened in Indian Territory on April 6, 1896, taking the name of William C. Page, a prominent Choctaw Indian.
evidence.quote: A post office was established at Page, Indian Territory on April 6, 1896.  It was named for William C. Page, a prominent Choctaw Indian.

evidence.claim: At its founding, the community lay in Wade County within the Choctaw Nation’s Apukshunnubbee District.
evidence.quote: At the time of its founding, Page was located in Wade County, a part of the Apukshunnubbee District of the Choctaw Nation.

evidence.claim: Heavener took a different course: Kansas City Southern bought its railway in 1900, then established a roundhouse in 1910 and made the town a division point.
evidence.quote: in 1900 when the Kansas City Southern Railway purchased the rail line. The company established a roundhouse in 1910, making Heavener a division point.

evidence.claim: In 1900 and 1901, a predecessor of the Arkansas Western Railroad added an eastward connection into Arkansas.
evidence.quote: In 1900-1901 a predecessor of the Arkansas Western Railroad constructed tracks from Heavener east into Arkansas.

evidence.claim: At its height the settlement held about 1,000 people, but the mill buildings do not survive as a town to explore.
evidence.quote: While at its height the population of the settlement was about 1,000, nothing remains of the old town today.

evidence.claim: From Heavener, the drive heads south on US 59 toward Stapp.
evidence.quote: It is located approximately eight miles south of Heavener on US Route 59.

evidence.claim: Along the way, Zoe lies just east of US 59/270, with the Black Fork of the Poteau River passing its north side.
evidence.quote: The community is on a county road just east of combined US routes 59-270. Heavener is approximately eight miles to the north. The Black Fork of the Poteau River flows past the north side of the community.

evidence.claim: Beyond Stapp, continue to Page, 5.5 miles west of the Arkansas border, on the combined highways.
evidence.quote: Page is located along U.S. routes 59 and 270, 5.5 miles (8.9 km) west of the Arkansas border.

evidence.claim: Side roads and neighboring scenic byways branch into the heavily forested mountains.
evidence.quote: Numerous side roads and other scenic byways invite the traveler to explore these heavily forested mountains.

flags: The cache supplies no road-building narrative, designation date or formal designation criteria. Overview uses documented corridor-community history and the tourism department’s scenic-byway description.
The nearly 2,600-foot elevation claim in current comes from an article grouping Mountain Gateway and Mountain Pass; omitted because it does not locate that elevation on this drive.
Page moment is shorter than 90 words because its cache page supplies only location, naming and historical jurisdiction.
Heavener source uses both Chocktaw and Choctaw; retained Choctaw Nation, the explicit jurisdictional name used in that source.
